planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated transplants after frost danger passes; this Sakata-bred intergeneric hybrid combines petunia flower size with calibrachoa's cleaner, less sticky foliage.

directions: SuperCal Premium Cinnamon carries a muted terracotta-brown bloom color unusual among bedding annuals, set against the self-cleaning, non-sticky foliage typical of this petunia-calibrachoa cross. It tolerates heat and heavy rain noticeably better than a standard petunia and keeps flowering weeks longer into fall. Grow in full sun in a fertile, well-drained container or bed mix and feed regularly to sustain bloom; no deadheading is required since spent flowers drop cleanly on their own.
sources: Sakata Seed America - SuperCal Petchoa Series
Proven Winners - SuperCal Premium Cinnamon Petchoa

planting.note: Seed-grown plants germinate readily in a warm mineral mix, but most growers instead root offsets or stem sections, which establish faster and keep the dense white covering of hair-like spines intact from the start.

directions: Cotton-top cactus is instantly recognizable for the dense covering of soft white, hair-like spines that swaddle its slender cylindrical stems, giving mature clustering specimens a shaggy, almost woolly appearance. Native to high-altitude sites in the Bolivian and Peruvian Andes, it tolerates cooler nights and brief light frost better than most columnar cacti from lower elevations. Grow in a very sharply drained mineral mix in full sun, and keep notably dry in winter, since the fuzzy spine covering traps moisture against the stem and encourages rot if the soil stays wet. Clusters of magenta-pink flowers appear near the stem tips once plants reach maturity.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant seed-propagated plugs after frost danger passes into consistently wet, humus-rich soil or shallow standing water; this PanAmerican Seed selection needs no pinching or growth regulators to hold its dense mounded shape.

directions: Live Wire is a breeder selection from PanAmerican Seed's ColorGrass line, bred specifically for a compact, uniform mound that stays tidy without pinching, unlike seed-grown fiber optic grass of mixed origin. The thread-fine foliage tipped in tiny pale flower spikelets gives the classic fiber-optic look, and the plant performs equally well as a container filler, a pond-margin accent in shallow water, or a houseplant kept consistently moist on a saucer. Keep the roots wet at all times; this selection does not tolerate drying out between waterings.
sources: PanAmerican Seed - ColorGrass Isolepis Live Wire
University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension - Fiber Optic Grass

planting.note: Set container transplants out after frost danger passes into well-drained soil in full sun; established plants tolerate considerable heat and some drought.

directions: This South African subshrub stays in near-continuous bloom through most of the growing season, covering its lobed, somewhat fleshy foliage in bright yellow daisy flowers held just above the leaf canopy. It builds into a rounded, loosely branched mound and responds well to a light shearing after each major flowering flush to keep growth dense rather than leggy. Plant in full sun with sharp drainage; it is a reliable perennial border and bedding shrub through zones 8-11 and a popular tender perennial container subject farther north.

planting.note: Plant once nighttime temperatures stay reliably warm, in well-drained soil that does not dry completely between waterings; reserve for frost-free zone 10-11 sites or large containers.

directions: Native to the sea cliffs of a few small Hawaiian islands off Molokai, this loulu palm is more compact and flowers at a younger age than most Pritchardia, making it a practical specimen palm for smaller gardens and large patio containers. Its broad, pleated fan leaves are often dusted with a fine silvery or grayish bloom on the underside, especially in young plants, giving it a distinct two-toned look in a breeze. Give it consistent warmth, full sun to light shade, and even moisture; it has no frost tolerance and should be moved under cover or into a protected microclimate if temperatures threaten to dip near freezing.
sources: International Palm Society - Palms journal species profiles

planting.note: Surface-sow on bare, disturbed soil in early spring in full sun; seed needs light and cool temperatures to germinate well.

directions: This pure-white-flowered selection of fireweed holds its clean color reliably from seed in good commercial strains, giving cut-flower and cottage growers a brighter alternative to the species' usual hot magenta spires. It shares the wild type's talent for colonizing open, disturbed ground and spreads readily by rhizome and wind-borne seed, so it reads best in a naturalized drift or a bed with firm edging rather than a tightly curated border. The tall flower spikes open from the base upward over several weeks in mid- to late summer and are a valued late-season source of nectar for bees.

planting.note: Set the clustering leaves shallowly in a very lean, sandy mineral mix so the flattened, translucent leaf tips sit nearly flush with the soil surface, in bright full sun.

directions: A close relative of the better-known Frithia pulchra, this species is distinguished by broader, more rounded leaf tips and a somewhat freer clustering habit over time. Native to grassland pockets in South Africa's Free State region, it survives among grass tussocks largely hidden except for the translucent windows at each leaf tip, which admit light to the buried photosynthetic tissue below. Pink to magenta daisy flowers open from the leaf centers in late summer. Grow exactly as for its cousin: a lean, fast-draining mineral mix, bright direct light, and water withheld except during active growth.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Start dormant scaly rhizomes shallowly in moist seed-starting mix once temperatures stay warm, keeping them in shade until shoots emerge.

directions: This Mexican gesneriad is distinguished from the closely related Eucodonia andrieuxii by its whorled leaf arrangement and lavender-purple, white-throated tubular flowers produced over a long summer season. It grows from the same type of small underground scaly rhizomes and has long been a favorite among gesneriad and African violet society members for easy windowsill culture. Keep it warm, shaded, and humid through active growth, then let it dry down and rest once foliage dies back for the winter, repotting the rhizomes fresh the following spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions or sow fresh seed in fall into moist, humus-rich woodland soil in shade; seed benefits from a cold winter stratification period before spring germination.

directions: A Pacific Northwest counterpart to the more widespread eastern Enemion biternatum, this species is native to shaded streambanks and moist woods west of the Cascades in Washington and Oregon. In late spring it sends up small white to pale rose flowers with five petal-like sepals above finely divided, fern-like foliage, then dies back to dormancy by midsummer heat. Grow in a humus-rich, consistently moist woodland bed in part shade, planting divisions or fall-sown seed alongside other spring ephemerals such as trillium and bleeding heart.

planting.note: Grow on a moss pole or bark slab in bright indirect light using a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix; this hemi-epiphytic climber needs support to develop its mature, more deeply cut leaf form.

directions: A smaller-growing relative of the better-known Amydrium medium, this Southeast Asian rainforest climber develops narrower, deeply pinnatifid leaves with a distinctive dissected, almost fern-like edge once it matures and begins climbing a support. In the juvenile stage leaves are simple and undivided, so the dramatic change in form as the plant ages is part of its appeal to collectors. Grow mounted on a moss pole or bark slab in bright indirect light with elevated humidity, letting the top inch of chunky aroid mix dry between waterings. All parts are toxic if ingested.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Mount on cork or grow in an open slatted basket, never a solid pot, since flower spikes emerge downward from the base of the pseudobulb and need open space below to hang freely.

directions: Native to Mexico and Central America, this Gongora is distinguished from the South American Gongora quinquenervis by the helmet-shaped hood on its flower column and typically paler, cream-to-yellow blooms finely spotted in reddish brown. Clustered ribbed pseudobulbs send up pendant flower racemes each summer that must be given open space below the plant to hang and display properly, which is why it is grown mounted or basket-grown rather than potted in a closed container. Provide bright, filtered light, regular watering through active growth, high humidity, and a brief, drier winter rest to encourage strong flowering the following season.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or small container vines after frost danger passes into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil with a trellis, obelisk, or fence to twine on.

directions: This selection of Brazilian firecracker vine, introduced through Plant Delights Nursery and named for horticulturist John Elsley, produces smaller, brighter scarlet-and-yellow tubular flowers on a twining habit that runs a bit more vigorously than typical seed-grown Manettia cordifolia. It blooms almost continuously from late spring through fall and is a dependable hummingbird draw for a trellis, mailbox post, or porch railing. In mild winters it can be root-hardy under heavy mulch as cold as the warmer parts of zone 8, though gardeners farther north typically grow it as a container plant or replace it annually.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery - Manettia cordifolia 'John Elsley'

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; it is extremely drought- and salt-tolerant once established but restricted to frost-free zone 10-11 landscapes.

directions: The largest species in its genus, this Hispaniola native carries a thick gray trunk and a dense, broad crown of stiff, blue-green fronds, giving it a far bulkier presence than the smaller Florida cherry palm already common in cultivation. Its common name comes from a traditional practice in Haiti and the Dominican Republic of tapping the trunk for a sweet sap once fermented into a local palm wine. Extremely tolerant of drought, wind, and salt spray once established, it makes a durable specimen for frost-free coastal landscapes, though slow growth and scarce nursery supply keep it mostly in the hands of palm collectors and botanical gardens.
sources: Montgomery Botanical Center palm collection notes

planting.note: Mount on a slab or grow in a shallow pan of fast-draining, humus-rich mix; roots establish readily from stem cuttings taken in spring.

directions: This long-cultivated Japanese form of the East Asian epiphytic gesneriad is distinguished from typical Lysionotus pauciflorus by slightly broader, glossier leaves and dependable sprays of lavender, purple-throated trumpet flowers in late summer and fall. In the wild it clings to mossy rock faces and tree trunks, so it performs best mounted on a slab or grown in a shallow pan of fast-draining, humus-rich mix rather than a deep pot. It tolerates light frost better than most gesneriads and can be overwintered in a cool greenhouse or an unheated but frost-free sunroom.

planting.note: Sow on a lean sand-and-peat fynbos mix kept just barely moist, never waterlogged, since this South African shrub rots quickly in boggy conditions typical of most carnivorous plant setups.

directions: A close relative of Roridula gorgonias from the same fynbos habitat of the Western Cape, this shrubby protocarnivore has narrower, more sharply toothed leaves and relies on the same resin-trap-and-assassin-bug partnership rather than true digestive enzymes to obtain nutrients from trapped insects. It is less commonly offered than its sister species but grown by the same specialist carnivorous plant nurseries and requires identical lean, fast-draining, winter-wet summer-dry conditions rather than a constant bog. Pale pink star-shaped flowers appear on older plants over a period of years, and the woody base can eventually form a substantial multi-stemmed shrub in a greenhouse or warm climate garden.

planting.note: Pot rooted offsets in spring with the swollen woody base held above the soil surface, in a sharply draining mineral succulent mix.

directions: Fockea crispa is a South African caudiciform vine in the milkweed family prized for its gnarled, bonsai-like gray trunk and wiry twining stems carrying small, slightly ruffled leaves. Collectors grow it with the trunk exposed well above the soil line to show off its sculptural form, in the same manner as its relative Fockea edulis, though its stems and trunk texture are more corky and deeply furrowed. It is slow to bulk up but extremely long-lived and drought-tolerant once mature, requiring water only during its active warm-season growth and almost none in winter dormancy. Grow it as a container specimen in full sun and bring it under cover well ahead of any frost, since it has essentially no cold tolerance.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant the brittle, spider-like fleshy roots in fall, spread horizontally about 4 in deep on a mound of sharply drained soil to keep the crown from sitting in winter moisture.

directions: The tallest commonly grown foxtail lily, this Central Asian species sends up massive bottle-brush flower spikes of soft pink blooms that can tower 8 to 9 feet above a basal rosette of broad, strap-like, blue-green leaves. It needs the same perfect drainage as smaller Eremurus species and hybrids, since its thick storage roots rot readily in heavy or wet soil, and the emerging spring foliage can be damaged by a late hard freeze. Because the foliage yellows and disappears soon after flowering, it is best planted among later-emerging perennials that can fill the visual gap it leaves behind in the border for the rest of the season.

planting.note: Mount on bark or grow in a slatted basket with coarse bark in bright, filtered light; this large-growing species needs more headroom than most Aerides as it matures.

directions: Lawrence's Aerides is a robust, broad-leaved vandaceous orchid from the Philippines, closely related to and sometimes confused with Aerides odorata but larger in every dimension, with thick, pendant racemes of waxy white flowers heavily blushed and spotted in rose-purple. It blooms reliably once mature and is valued by growers for the sheer density and fragrance of its hanging flower chains, which can carry dozens of blooms on a single spike. Give it strong, filtered light, good year-round humidity, and a pronounced seasonal dip in watering during its short winter rest to encourage flowering the following season.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in a well-drained cactus mix after the cut end has calloused for several days; this species is widely used as understock for grafting epiphyllums and other soft-stemmed cacti.

directions: A slender, gray-green, vigorously growing columnar cactus of uncertain wild origin, long cultivated mainly as a hardy, rot-resistant grafting stock for epiphyllums, rhipsalis, and other soft-stemmed cactus relatives that struggle on their own roots. Left ungrafted, it also makes an attractive garden specimen in its own right, producing large, fragrant, night-blooming white flowers typical of its Harrisia relatives. It tolerates brief light frost better than many true tropical cacti and grows quickly in full sun with sharply drained soil, making it a forgiving choice for collectors who also want functional grafting material on hand.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Mount on bark or grow in a shallow, fast-draining basket in bright, filtered light with a cooler, drier winter rest than most cattleya-alliance relatives.

directions: The sister species to the better-known Rhyncholaelia digbyana, this compact Central American epiphyte carries the same waxy, succulent, powdery blue-green foliage but produces smaller, pale greenish-white flowers with a less dramatically fringed lip and a lighter, sweeter evening fragrance. Like its relative, it has been used by breeders to pass fragrance and a distinctive lip shape into hybrid Cattleya and Brassavola crosses. It wants a cooler and drier winter rest than most of its warmth-loving cattleya relatives, along with strong light and excellent air movement around the roots, and resents being kept constantly wet.

planting.note: Let a broken-off stem section callus for a couple of days, then press it shallowly into a very gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in bright light.

directions: Like its relative Duvalia sulcata, this South African stapeliad forms a congested low mat of small, four-angled, finger-like stems that stay close to the soil, but its flowers are smaller, more deeply textured, and a darker brownish-purple with a distinctly warty surface. It is grown in the same way as other Duvalia and Stapelia relatives, in a shallow pan with extremely sharp drainage and bright light tempered by a little midday shade in hot climates. Flowers release a faint carrion scent to attract fly pollinators and open flush against the stem clusters rather than on raised stalks. Withhold water almost entirely through winter dormancy to avoid rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; this smaller Bellevalia naturalizes readily in a rock garden or bulb lawn setting.

directions: A compact Caucasus-region bulb related to the larger, better-known Giant Grape Hyacinth, this species produces dense, cylindrical racemes of small, deep violet-black flowers held just above a modest tuft of narrow basal leaves in early-to-mid spring. It is easy and reliable in a sunny, sharply drained rock garden or front-of-border planting, increasing slowly by offsets without becoming aggressive, and pairs well with other small spring bulbs such as crocus and dwarf iris. Specialty fall-bulb nurseries carry it as a novelty alternative to common grape hyacinth for collectors wanting something less ubiquitous.

planting.note: Anchor stem cuttings or the plantlets that form on broken-off leaves into nutrient-rich aquarium substrate; new roots and plantlets form readily from both stems and leaf fragments.

directions: One of the most popular background and midground plants in the freshwater aquarium hobby, this Southeast Asian wetland species is notable for its variable, deeply lobed to almost lacy leaves, which can look markedly different depending on light intensity and whether the plant is grown submersed or emersed. It grows quickly under moderate aquarium lighting without requiring CO2 injection, though added CO2 and root tab fertilizer produce denser, more compact growth and richer leaf dissection. Broken leaf fragments readily sprout new plantlets, making it one of the easiest aquarium plants to propagate, and regular topping of tall stems keeps plantings full rather than leggy.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, ideally in a large container or behind a root barrier; this cultivar is far less vigorous and less prone to escaping than the plain green species.

directions: This classic variegated selection of giant reed carries crisp white-and-green striped canes that make it a long-standing favorite architectural accent for large containers and borders, clump-forming rather than running aggressively like the invasive plain green species it derives from. It reverts occasionally to plain green growth, which should be cut out at the base promptly to keep the variegation strong, and it is noticeably less cold-hardy and less vigorous overall than straight Arundo donax, rarely becoming a weed problem where it is grown. Cut old canes back hard in late winter before new spring growth begins, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor and clean variegation.

planting.note: Plant grafted, container-grown trees in spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral loam in full sun; stake the leading shoot while young to establish the height before the weeping habit takes over.

directions: This distinctive weeping cultivar of giant sequoia produces narrow, often contorted or snaking leaders clothed in drooping, rope-like branches instead of the broad, classically pyramidal form of the wild species, giving mature specimens a sculptural, almost surreal silhouette unlike any other conifer. Young plants are frequently trained with a stake to establish an upright leader before the pendulous branching habit is allowed to develop freely, and the ultimate shape varies considerably from tree to tree depending on how it is trained when young. It shares the species' deep, fibrous, fire-resistant bark and general toughness, and makes a striking specimen tree for large gardens and arboreta in zones 6 through 8 where summer heat is not extreme.

planting.note: Plant the fragile, finger-shaped tubers horizontally about 4 in deep after the last frost, handling gently to avoid snapping them, and provide a trellis for the climbing tendrils.

directions: This is the classic large-flowered selection of gloriosa lily, long grown as cut flowers and garden climbers for its exceptionally bold, wavy-edged petals in rich crimson-red fading to golden yellow at the base, a more vivid and consistent color break than the variable wild species typically shows. It climbs by tendril-tipped leaf tips rather than twining stems, so a trellis, netting, or nearby shrub is needed for support as the thin stems lengthen through summer. Every part of the plant is highly toxic if eaten, so it should be sited well away from children, pets, and livestock. Where winters drop below zone 8, lift and dry the tubers after foliage yellows and store them in barely damp peat at 50 to 60°F until spring.

planting.note: set divisions into shaded crevices once hard frosts have passed

directions: This sport of the species carries cream-and-green marbled succulent leaves that flush pink in cold weather, so propagate only by division or leaf cuttings since seedlings revert to plain green. Arching sprays of small yellow flowers appear over the mat in early summer. Grow it in gritty, humus-rich soil in a shaded wall crevice or rockery where it can trail over an edge.

planting.note: sow fresh seed outdoors in autumn so winter cold breaks dormancy

directions: Give this spine-tipped tussock full sun and sharply drained, lean soil, as in its native New Zealand high country. The rigid golden-bronze rosette of needle-sharp leaves takes several years to build before sending up a dramatic flowering spike. Handle mature plants with gloves, since the foliage tips are genuinely sharp enough to puncture skin.

planting.note: tuck divisions into shaded rock crevices with sharp drainage after frost

directions: Set rosettes into a shaded, north-facing crevice or vertical crack with gritty, humus-rich soil, recreating the shaded Balkan limestone cliffs where the species grows wild. This white-flowered selection sends up clusters of pure white, nodding blooms above the fuzzy evergreen rosettes in late spring. The foliage can curl and appear shriveled in drought, then rehydrate and green up again once watered, a resurrection trait the species is known for.

planting.note: divide and transplant dormant crowns in early fall or very early spring

directions: Plant divisions in humus-rich, consistently moist woodland soil in dappled shade, where this very slow-spreading perennial will eventually form a tidy clump. Tiny yellow-centered flowers surrounded by lime-green bracts open in late winter before the crisply white-and-green variegated leaves expand. Because it resents disturbance, leave established clumps undivided for several years once sited.

planting.note: repot divisions into fast-draining bark mix just as new growth emerges

directions: Grow in a well-drained bark mix with warm temperatures and bright, filtered light, watering freely while the pleated leaves are actively growing. This Amazonian species is unusual among orchids for its twisted, lopsided flowers, which lack the mirror symmetry seen in nearly every other orchid genus. Once the canes lose their leaves the plant enters a dry, leafless rest, and watering should be cut back sharply until new growth resumes.

planting.note: Set out after frost danger has passed into a moist, part-shade bed or large container near a wall for winter protection

directions: This Mexican volcanic-belt native grows naturally along seepages and shaded rock faces in oak forest, so it wants consistently damp soil and relief from hot midday sun. Give it filtered shade or morning sun with afternoon shelter, and mulch the fleshy roots heavily where winters dip near freezing since the species dies back but often resprouts from the base. Pinch young growth to encourage branching and more of the long, waxy red-and-green pendant blooms that draw hummingbirds through summer and fall.

planting.note: Move outdoors into partial shade once nights stay above the mid-40s F; in marginal zones grow in a large pot that can be sheltered over winter

directions: Unlike the familiar hanging-basket hybrids, this Mexican and Guatemalan species grows into a genuine small evergreen tree with glossy foliage and upright, lilac-like clusters of pink to white flowers instead of the usual pendant blooms. Plant it in humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade or morning sun and keep roots evenly moist through the growing season. It tolerates light frost to the upper 20s F but top growth is damaged below freezing, so container culture is the safer route outside zone 10.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Plant into part-shade beds after frost risk passes, or keep potted and bring under cover for winter

directions: Found from southern Mexico into Panama in open forest margins at elevation, this small-statured species carries tiny tubular flowers on fine, airy stems rather than the showy blooms of its hybrid cousins. It wants light, fertile soil that stays evenly moist and a position in partial shade, and sheds its leaves readily if stressed by drought or cold. Treat it as a tender perennial in most of the US, growing it outdoors in summer and overwintering in a frost-free spot further north.

planting.note: Move divisions or potted stock outdoors into deep shade only after night temperatures stay reliably above 50 F

directions: Native to the humid forest floor of southern Mexico, Guatemala, and Honduras, this begonia builds a thick upright rhizome and fans of palmate, hand-sized leaves that scorch quickly in direct sun. Grow it in bright, indirect light or deep dappled shade with rich, well-drained soil kept consistently moist but never soggy. Dense heads of soft pink flowers appear on tall stalks from late winter into spring, and the plant is equally happy as a shaded patio container specimen or houseplant where winters are too cold for it outdoors.

planting.note: Set out in a wind-sheltered, partly shaded spot once temperatures hold above 45 F; bring indoors well before first frost

directions: This large Central American shrub, native to the understories of Costa Rica, Nicaragua, and Panama, produces showy coral-orange bracts and pink-and-orange tubular flowers on arching stems. It performs best in humus-rich, well-drained soil under partial shade to full shade, with steady moisture and protection from cold wind. Where winters drop below the mid-40s F it should be grown in a container and moved to a bright, sheltered location rather than left outdoors.

planting.note: Plant tuberous divisions in dappled shade once soil has warmed; expect foliage to die back completely each winter

directions: Native to seasonally dry tropical forest from Mexico to Honduras, this tuberous spiderwort forms low mounds of thick, glossy succulent leaves that can look almost translucent when backlit. It grows from an underground tuber and goes dormant in winter, so it tolerates being dry at rest but wants regular moisture and dappled shade through its summer growth and bloom period of small pink flowers. In cold climates, lift and store the tuber over winter or grow it in a container that can be kept frost-free.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Grow year-round in a shaded container; set outside only in warm, shaded, frost-free weather

directions: This small Mexican highland peperomia grows from a persistent fleshy tuber and sends up round, umbrella-like leaves on wiry stalks each rainy season, dying back to the tuber during the dry winter. In shade the foliage lifts up on its stems to catch filtered light, while brighter, drier conditions keep it low and flattened against the soil. Pot it in a gritty, humus-rich mix, water generously while in leaf, and let it rest nearly dry once the tuber goes dormant.
sources: Huntington Botanical Gardens International Succulent Introductions (ISI)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant, terrarium climber, or shaded hanging specimen; only set outside seasonally in essentially frost-free, humid climates

directions: A climbing gesneriad from the high-elevation cloud forests of Ecuador, this species naturally scrambles up tree trunks in deep, humid shade and needs that same filtered light and constant moisture in cultivation. Pot it in a chunky, well-aerated mix, provide a moss pole or similar support for the vining stems, and keep humidity high with regular misting or a terrarium setting. It thrives at cool-to-moderate indoor temperatures and resents both direct sun and dry air, making it best suited to shaded greenhouse, terrarium, or houseplant culture outside the tropics.

planting.note: Nick or soak hard seed coat before sowing; resents root disturbance so direct-sow or use deep pots.

directions: This iconic inland-Australian wildflower produces trailing stems lined with soft gray-green leaves and startling large flowers, each a glossy black boss set against a vivid scarlet-red hood. Scarify or soak the hard seed coat before sowing, since untreated seed germinates slowly and erratically, and place plants where drainage is excellent since the species is highly prone to rot in humid or waterlogged soil. Grown as a warm-season annual outside true desert climates, it is usually direct-sown after the soil has warmed because seedlings dislike transplanting. The nectar-rich flowers are visited by honeyeaters and native bees, making it a striking addition to a dry, sun-baked native bed.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in lean, fast-draining soil; seed propagation is unreliable due to a hard, waxy pyrene coat.

directions: Spotted emu bush is a wide-ranging arid-zone shrub whose tubular, speckled flowers come in shades from deep red to orange, pink, and yellow depending on the form, each bloom marked inside with darker spots or blotches. It is propagated almost exclusively from cuttings, since the hard-coated seed germinates slowly and unpredictably even with treatment. Once established in lean, sharply drained soil it tolerates long dry spells and reflected heat, flowering heaviest in the warmer months. The nectar draws honeyeaters in its native range and is readily visited by bees in cultivated gardens.

planting.note: Plant cutting-grown stock in well-drained soil; prostrate forms spread wide and root along trailing stems.

directions: Common emu bush ranges from low, wide-spreading groundcover forms to small rounded shrubs, all covered for much of the year in curved, tubular flowers in yellow, orange, red, or maroon depending on the selection. It is propagated from cuttings taken from selected prostrate or compact forms, since the species is extremely variable across its wide range and named clones breed true only vegetatively. Established plants shrug off heat, drought, and poor sandy soils, making it a durable choice for a dry bank or rock garden. The flowers are a reliable nectar source for honeyeaters and bees through most of the growing season.

planting.note: Press seed onto the soil surface since light aids germination; also establishes readily from division.

directions: Common everlasting forms a low, spreading mat of soft silver-gray foliage topped for most of the warmer months with small, long-lasting, papery-bracted yellow button flowers. It is one of the easiest Australian native daisies to raise from seed, germinating readily when pressed into the surface of a free-draining mix, and it can also be split and replanted from existing clumps. Extremely drought tolerant once rooted in, it is widely used as a tough, low-maintenance groundcover and erosion-control planting as well as a garden border plant. The flowers draw small native bees and butterflies throughout the bloom season.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or cutting-grown stock in lean, well-drained soil; seed can be slow and benefits from smoke-water treatment.

directions: In late spring this wiry, fine-leaved shrub smothers itself in masses of small, star-shaped white-to-pink flowers, each petal ending in the fine, bristle-like fringe on the sepals that gives the plant its common name. It is widespread across the drier woodlands and heath of southern Australia and tolerates poor, rocky, or sandy soils as long as drainage is sharp. Named forms are usually propagated from cuttings for reliability, though species seed can be grown with patience and benefits from smoke-water treatment to break dormancy. The abundant small flowers are a strong draw for native bees during their spring peak.

planting.note: Plant cutting-grown stock in lean, sandy, well-drained soil; prune lightly after flowering to keep growth dense.

directions: Rock thryptomene is a fine-textured Western Australian shrub that covers its wiry branches in winter and early spring with countless tiny, five-petaled pink or white flowers, giving a long-distance effect like a haze of color over the foliage. Commercial plants are grown from cuttings, since this keeps named flower-color forms consistent and sidesteps the slow, uneven germination typical of small Myrtaceae seed. It needs the same lean, sharply drained, slightly acidic soil favored by most heath-country natives and resents heavy or wet ground. The long-blooming flowers are a valuable late-winter nectar source for native bees and are also popular as a cut flower.

planting.note: Plant cutting-grown stock in moist but well-drained soil; tolerates more cold and moisture than most Australian shrub natives.

directions: Native to the cool highlands and forest margins of southeastern Australia and Tasmania, dusty daisy bush is one of the more cold-tolerant Australian shrubs, smothering itself each spring in masses of small daisy flowers in white, mauve, pink, or blue depending on the form, set against soft, gray-green, faintly aromatic foliage. Because color forms vary considerably from seed, named selections are propagated from cuttings to keep flower color true. It prefers more moisture and richer soil than most Australian natives and appreciates light shade in hot inland climates, which has made it a long-favored shrub in mild coastal gardens outside Australia as well. The dense spring flower display is heavily visited by bees and butterflies.
